newsitem.title: CHINA: China considers tax reforms to boost car sales.
newsitem.headline: China considers tax reforms to boost car sales.

text.p: China is considering cutting taxes imposed on car owners by local governments to help boost business for automobile manufacturers, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday.
The newspaper said car owners are subject to a tangle of more than 20 fees and taxes in place in most parts of China, many of which may be illegal.

"Through the reform, proposed by several ministries and commissions, major taxes and fees levied on motor vehicles, especially sedans, are expected to become a single tax, the so-called fuel consumption tax," the newspaper said.

The southern island province of Hainan has adopted a new simplified car tax structure in line with international conventions which is viewed as a successful model for other parts of the country, it said.
It quoted an official as saying the new proposed fuel consumption tax was also aimed at putting pressure on auto makers to develop and manufacture more efficient, energy-saving vehicles.
It said no timetable had been set for the implementation of the tax.
China is also looking to expand car leasing companies to allow firms and individuals to use cars when necessaary even if they can't afford to buy one, the newspaper said.

It said there were now more than 50 car lease companies in operation across China, and quoted a domestic trade official as saying development of the market also provided wide opportunities for manufacturers to supply cars and vans.
"Now is the time to develop the automobile leasing industry to meet the demands of both the manufacturers and customers," it quoted the official as saying.
The newspaper said China's car output is expected to hit 1.5 million per year by 2000, which will require an expansion of the private car market.
Turnover of the car leasing business in China is currently less than one percent of that in the United States, providing huge room for growth, he added.
